title: Gotthard pass road and Tremola
place: Göschenen through the Schöllenen gorge, Andermatt and Hospental over the pass and down the Val Tremola to Airolo
summary: A mule path became a carriage road: the cantons on the Gotthard route built a 6 m wide road from Göschenen to Airolo, with the famous bends of the Tremola.
why: For centuries only a mule path crossed the Gotthard. In 1707 the engineer Pietro Morettini cut the Urnerloch, a 60 m tunnel in the Schöllenen gorge. It replaced the Twärren bridge, a wooden walkway hung on the rock face. The Urnerloch was one of the first tunnels in the Alps.

Around 1800 the mule path was in a bad state. The new Simplon road (1805) and the roads over the Splügen and San Bernardino (1818–1823) took traffic away. In 1826 Lucerne, Uri, Basel, Solothurn and Ticino signed an agreement to build a road for coaches and carts.

The road was to be 6 m wide, with a maximum gradient of 10%. Uri built its part in 1828–1830, Ticino the Tremola part in 1828–1832. Engineer Francesco Meschini planned it. Where it could, the road followed the old mule path. After the Gotthard railway (1882) and the road tunnel (1980) the pass road lost most of its traffic.
gained: From 1831 coaches carried post and people. From 1842 a daily coach ran between Chiasso and Flüelen. In winter post sleighs crossed the pass.
Around 1870 an estimated 70,000 travellers and 10,000 to 20,000 t of goods crossed the pass by road per year.
The Urnerloch made the wooden Twärren bridge in the Schöllenen gorge unnecessary.
lost: The road followed the mule path for most of the way and replaced it. Today only short pieces of the mule path remain.
In 1832 Uri ended the old transport rights of the local muleteer cooperatives and allowed free competition.
Most of the 1830 road in Uri was later rebuilt with modern mortared walls. Only a few original pieces remain.

title: Simplon pass road (Napoleon's road)
place: Brig/Glis over the Simplon Pass to Gondo and on to Domodossola (Italy)
summary: On Napoleon's order, engineers built the first modern carriage road over the high Alps, from Glis over the Simplon to Domodossola.
why: Before 1800 only a mule path crossed the Simplon. After Kaspar Stockalper fell in 1678, the pass lost its international traffic and the path decayed. Napoleon saw the Simplon as the shortest link between Paris and Milan. He wanted a road that was usable for cannons (big guns).

Napoleon ordered the road in 1800. Work under the army made little progress. In 1801 the road engineer Nicolas Céard took control. Up to 3000 workers built the road. It opened on 9 October 1805, a few months late. Napoleon himself never crossed the Simplon.

The road had eight large bridges and seven galleries (short tunnels). Travellers admired it, but the railways took away its traffic. After the Simplon rail tunnel opened in 1906, travellers fell from 13,258 (1905) to 845 (1907). From 1957 the road was rebuilt for cars. Since 1960 it is the national road A9.
gained: The Simplon became the shortest and clearly the fastest link between Paris and Milan.
A coach post started soon after the opening. In winter it used horse sleighs until 1953–1954.
The road was up to 7.2 m and even 8.4 m wide, so two carts could pass each other easily.
The road was seen as a wonder of technology. Many travellers came to see it in the early 19th century.
lost: From 1957 the road was rebuilt. The new road mostly follows Napoleon's line, and so it destroyed most of the old road.
The rebuilt road brought much heavy traffic. In 2010 about 80,000 lorries per year crossed the pass.
Avalanches, rockfall and the weather damaged the road. In 1821 a traveller saw many broken granite posts along its edge.

title: San Bernardino and Splügen carriage roads
place: From Splügen over the San Bernardino Pass to Mesocco, and from Splügen over the Splügen Pass towards Chiavenna (Italy)
summary: Two new roads for carts and coaches replaced the mule paths over the San Bernardino and the Splügen and made the Graubünden passes busy transit routes.
why: Before 1818 local cooperatives of muleteer farmers, the Porten, carried the goods over the passes. Each Porte had its own section. A short paved road over the San Bernardino from about 1770 was soon given up again.

From 1818 to 1823 two carriage roads were built at the same time. The Kingdom of Lombardy–Venetia built and paid the Splügen road (1818–1822), so that transit would not move to the San Bernardino. The San Bernardino road was paid mainly by Sardinia–Piedmont, the Chur transport guild and the canton. On the San Bernardino the builder moved the Rhine bridge up the valley and led the bends away from avalanche slopes.

Freight and tourism grew strongly. Traffic was highest in the mid-1850s. After the Gotthard railway opened in 1882, traffic over the Graubünden passes almost stopped. Both passes are closed in winter since the Second World War.
gained: For the first time freight carts and coaches could cross the San Bernardino all the way.
The new San Bernardino road avoided the avalanche slopes that the old path crossed near Hinterrhein.
Freight increased strongly and tourism started. Carters, innkeepers, craftsmen and farmers earned money from the transit.
The Splügen road of 1818–1822 is still in use, in summer as a quick link to Lake Como.
lost: The muleteer cooperatives (Porten) lost their work. They were finally abolished in 1861, against their resistance.
In 1834 a storm destroyed most of the first Splügen road in the Hüscherenbach gorge. The road was moved further west.
On the Italian side of the Splügen, widening works are destroying the old stone avalanche galleries.

title: Melide causeway (Ponte Diga) across Lake Lugano
place: Across Lake Lugano between Melide and Bissone
summary: An 817 m dam across Lake Lugano carried first the road, from 1874 the railway and from the late 1960s the motorway.
why: Before the 19th century the Gotthard transit tried to go around Lake Lugano, which is long and surrounded by mountains. After the cantonal road was built in 1818, a ferry crossed the lake from Melide from 1819.
From 1844 to 1847 the canton built a dam across the lake from Melide to Bissone. It was built on a moraine (a ridge of glacier rubble) on the lake floor. It was first a road causeway.
The railway has used the dam since 1874 and the motorway A2 since the late 1960s. The dam made the lake area the main route through Ticino.
gained: Road traffic could cross the lake without a ferry.
The lake area became the preferred route for road, railway (1874) and motorway (1968–1970) through Ticino.
lost: The ferry from Melide, in service since 1819, stopped in 1847 after the dam was built.
The dam now divides Lake Lugano into a northern and a southern basin.

title: Spanisch-Brötli-Bahn Zurich–Baden, the first Swiss railway
place: Limmat valley from Zurich main station via Altstetten, Schlieren and Dietikon to Baden
summary: In 1847 the Swiss Northern Railway opened the line from Zurich to Baden, the first railway line built on Swiss soil.
why: Before 1847, people and goods went from Zurich to Baden by road or by boat. A railway line from Zurich to Basel was planned. The Swiss Northern Railway (Schweizerische Nordbahn) took over plans of an older Basel–Zurich company in 1846.

The engineer Alois Negrelli planned and built the line in 1845–1847. The first train ran in August 1847 through the Limmat valley at about 30 km/h. People soon called it the Spanisch-Brötli-Bahn, because a Baden pastry (Spanisch Brötli) could now arrive fresh in Zurich.

The line stopped at Baden. The cantons of Aargau and the two Basel refused the concessions (permits) to build further. The Northern Railway joined the new Swiss Northeastern Railway (NOB) in 1853. The NOB took the line on via Brugg to Aarau in 1856–1858.
gained: The opening train needed 45 minutes from Zurich to Baden, with 140 invited guests on board.
The HLS says that railways created the Swiss home market and linked the Swiss economy to the European market. This first line was the start of that network.
lost: The HLS says that railways often made peripheral (remote) regions lose out, while the centres gained. This is a general statement for all Swiss railways, not only for this line.

title: Hauenstein tunnels (1858 and base tunnel 1916)
place: Jura crossing of the Basel–Olten line: first tunnel Läufelfingen–Trimbach, base tunnel Tecknau–Olten
summary: Two rail tunnels took the Basel–Olten line through the Jura at the Hauenstein: the first in 1858, the 8.1 km base tunnel in 1916.
why: The Hauenstein passes were old routes over the Jura between Basel and Olten. A new pass road was built in 1827–1829. The Central Railway (Centralbahn) then built the line from Basel to Olten through the Hauenstein.
The first tunnel, about 2.5 km long, runs between Läufelfingen and Trimbach. In 1857 a fire broke out in a wooden shaft during the work, and 64 people died. The tunnel was finished in 1857/1858.
In 1912–1915 a second, 8134 m long base tunnel was built lower down, from Tecknau to near Olten. It opened in 1916.
gained: The tunnels gave Basel a direct rail link to Olten and the Swiss Plateau.
The base tunnel made the line flatter. The old line via Läufelfingen stayed in use as a regional line.
lost: 64 people died in the fire of 1857 in the first tunnel.
The railway, mainly the first tunnel of 1857, brought a massive drop in traffic over the Upper Hauenstein pass.

title: Axenstrasse along Lake Uri
place: East shore of Lake Uri (Urnersee) between Flüelen, Sisikon and Brunnen
summary: A road blasted into the cliffs of the Axen closed the last gap of the Gotthard road and linked Uri by land with Schwyz.
why: The almost vertical cliffs of the Axen blocked the land route between Flüelen and Brunnen. Most traffic went by boat. A path over the mountain existed, but it was dangerous and perhaps not always passable. In 1799 the Russian general Suvorov did not take his army over the Axen.

After the Gotthard road was finished in the 1830s, a link from Flüelen to Brunnen was the next step. Plans existed from 1837, but Uri feared the cost. Only with money from the federal state and for military reasons did Uri start. The Gotthard, the national Alpine fortress, was to be easy to reach.
Work started on 6 October 1862 in Flüelen. In 1864 Sisikon was reachable by road for the first time. On 3 July 1865 the whole road from Brunnen to Flüelen opened.
gained: From 1865 the Gotthard route could be driven by road the whole way.
Sisikon, a village of Uri, got its first road link with Flüelen in 1864.
Schwyz and the large towns of the Swiss plateau were suddenly within easy reach of the Reuss valley.
With its views and its bold rock galleries, the road became a world-famous tourist attraction.
lost: The steamboats on the lake lost most of their goods traffic to the new road.
The road cost 842,000 francs. Uri paid 598,000 francs for its part, partly with loans; the federal state gave 290,000 francs.
Since 1976–1977 new tunnels and galleries were built. Several sections of the 1865 road were closed or became footpaths.

title: Vitznau–Rigi railway, the first mountain rack railway in Europe
place: From Vitznau on Lake Lucerne via Rigi Kaltbad and Staffel to Rigi Kulm
summary: In 1871 the Vitznau–Rigi railway of Niklaus Riggenbach opened as the first rack railway up a mountain in Europe; it reached Rigi Kulm in 1873.
why: Tourists came to the Rigi from about 1800. The first inn on Rigi Kulm opened in 1816, and more hotels followed. A path from Weggis up the Rigi was built in 1818–1820, and local people carried travellers and goods up the mountain.

The engineer Niklaus Riggenbach patented a system with a toothed wheel and a rack rail in 1863. With the engineers Zschokke and Naeff he got the concession (permit) from the canton of Lucerne in 1869. The first train ran on 21 May 1871, but only to the cantonal border at Staffelhöhe. The Schwyz side built the line on to Rigi Kulm and leased it to the Vitznau company in 1873.
In 1875 a second rack railway from Arth-Goldau to Rigi Kulm followed.
gained: The railways brought more visitors. In 1880 the two Rigi railways carried almost 140,000 passengers, in 1910 a good 180,000.
Today the Rigi has more than 900,000 visitors a year. The rack rails of 1871 are still in use.
lost: Until 1871 many people of Weggis earned money as porters on the Rigi path. The railway took away this work.
In Arth, the Arth–Rigi railway of 1875 also brought loss of income to many inhabitants.

title: Gotthard railway and Gotthard tunnel
place: Reuss valley from Erstfeld via Wassen and Göschenen, tunnel to Airolo, Leventina down to Biasca
summary: From 1872 to 1882 the Gotthard railway company built the first Swiss rail crossing of the Alps, with a 15 km tunnel from Göschenen to Airolo.
why: The idea of a rail line through the Gotthard came up in the middle of the 19th century. In 1863 a Gotthard association, led by Alfred Escher, was founded with the support of 15 cantons and two railway companies. In 1869 the Gotthard route was chosen over other Alpine crossings.

The Gotthard railway company was founded in Lucerne in 1871. The Geneva engineer Louis Favre won the contract for the tunnel. Dynamite was used for the first time in tunnel building here. Costs and delays brought the company into a crisis from 1875. To save money, the ramps were made steeper, with tighter curves, and with only one track. Near Wassen and in the Leventina the line climbs in loops and spiral tunnels.

Through traffic started in 1882. Goods and part of the passengers now went mainly over the Gotthard axis. The Swiss Federal Railways (SBB) took over the line in 1909. The full double track was only finished in 1965.
gained: The line was the first rail crossing of the Alps in Switzerland. Goods and part of the passenger traffic moved to the Gotthard axis.
The HLS says that faster railways made space shrink and distances smaller. The Gotthard line shortened the trip between northern Switzerland and Italy.
lost: Many workers died. The HLS gives 177 deaths for the summit tunnel alone; SRF gives 199 official deaths for the first Gotthard rail tunnel and says the real number was probably higher.
During the building, the miners rose up for higher wages and better working conditions.
After the Gotthard tunnel opened in 1882, goods traffic over the passes of Graubünden collapsed (HLS, article on the Rhaetian Railway).

title: Pilatus railway, the steepest rack railway in the world
place: From Alpnachstad on Lake Alpnach via Ämsigen and the Eselwand to Pilatus Kulm
summary: From 1886 to 1889 a rack railway with slopes of up to 48% was built from Alpnachstad to Pilatus Kulm; it is still the steepest rack railway in the world.
why: Tourism on the Pilatus began in 1856–1861 with the Hotel Klimsenhorn. The engineer Eduard Locher had the idea of a railway up the mountain. Many people thought he was mad.

The line was built from 1886 to 1889. Normal rack systems could not work on such steep slopes, because the toothed wheels could climb out of the rack. Locher made a special system with two horizontal toothed wheels. It was shown at the world exhibition in Paris in 1889.
The line opened in 1889. It is 4618 m long. Steam railcars ran until 1937; then the line was electrified.
gained: Before electrification about 50,000 people a year used the railway; after 1937 more than 100,000. Today almost 300,000 guests a year ride up.
The Hotel Pilatus-Kulm was built in 1890, one year after the railway opened.

stops.title: Straight up the mountain
text: This map shows the line 16 years after the opening. It climbs from Alpnachstad through the forest to the Ämsigen alp, where trains can pass.
The last part runs along the Eselwand rock face to Pilatus Kulm.

stops.title: Still the steepest
text: With up to 48% slope it is still the steepest rack railway in the world. The trip takes 30 to 40 minutes.

title: Klausen pass road
place: Altdorf through the Schächental over the Klausen Pass and the Urnerboden to Linthal
summary: A military road over the Klausen Pass linked Uri and Glarus and gave the army a route along the northern Alps.
why: Before the road, the Klausen had only a mule path of local importance. Glarus wanted a link to the Gotthard route since the 1860s. The army general staff wanted a road along the first ridge of the northern Alps. Troops could then move between the Aare, Reuss and Linth valleys.

In 1892 the assemblies of Glarus and Uri decided to build the road. The federal state paid 80% of the costs. Work began in Uri in 1893 and in Glarus in 1895. The road opened to traffic on 21 August 1899; the official opening was on 10 June 1900.

The ground was unstable and wet in many places. The tunnels had to be lined with stone. Costs were 80% higher than planned. People in the upper Schächental opposed the road; their representatives said it would only bring discontent and idleness.
gained: Uri and Glarus got a road link. A coach service started in 1900; because it was successful, a second one started in 1901.
The army got a road for moving troops between the Reuss and Linth valleys.
After the road opened, the people of Urigen turned more towards Unterschächen in their daily life.
lost: Many building firms forced their workers to buy food in the firms' own stores at too high prices.
The road cost 80% more than planned. The federal state also paid 80% of the extra costs.
Above Unterschächen a new line was built against the bitter resistance of local people.
Since the 1980s parts of the road were widened. Concrete walls replace the old stone walls.

title: Jungfrau railway to the Jungfraujoch
place: From Kleine Scheidegg via Eigergletscher, then in a tunnel through the Eiger and Mönch to the Jungfraujoch
summary: From 1896 to 1912 Adolf Guyer-Zeller's company built an electric rack railway, mostly in a tunnel through the Eiger and Mönch, up to the Jungfraujoch at 3454 m.
why: The Zurich industrialist Adolf Guyer-Zeller wanted to open up the Jungfrau massif with an electric rack railway. The aim was tourism in the high Alps.

Building started on 27 July 1896 at Kleine Scheidegg. The stations opened step by step: Eigergletscher in 1898, Eigerwand in 1903, Eismeer in 1905. The tunnel reached the Jungfraujoch on 21 February 1912, and the line opened on 1 August 1912.
The line is 9.3 km long, and about 7.1 km run inside the Eiger and the Mönch. The last part up to the Jungfrau summit was never built, partly because money was short.
gained: At the start of the 21st century about one million tourists a year visited the Jungfraujoch, the highest railway station in Europe.
A research station has worked on the Jungfraujoch since 1931, and the Sphinx observatory since 1937.
lost: 30 workers died while the line was built, most of them in blasting accidents.
The workers went on strike six times, because the working conditions were very hard.

stops.title: Into the Eiger
text: This map shows the line three years after the opening. From Kleine Scheidegg it runs in the open to the Eiger glacier station.
Then the tunnel (dashed on the old map) climbs inside the Eiger and the Mönch to the Jungfraujoch.

stops.title: Top of Europe
text: Today the trains take visitors from many countries up to the Jungfraujoch all year.

title: Simplon tunnel
place: Rail tunnel from Brig (Valais) under the Simplon massif to Iselle (Italy)
summary: From 1898 to 1906 a 19.8 km rail tunnel was dug from Brig to Iselle; at its opening it was the longest rail tunnel in the world.
why: Since 1805 a road built on the order of Napoleon led over the Simplon pass. In the Simplon treaties of 1895 Switzerland and Italy agreed on a rail tunnel. Building and running it was given to the Jura-Simplon railway.

Work started in 1898. Brittle rock and mountain water slowed the work. Rock and water reached more than 50 °C. The engineers dug two single-track tunnels with regular links between them, for air, and they cooled the work sites with sprayed water.
The Swiss Federal Railways (SBB) took over the Jura-Simplon railway and completed the tunnel in 1906.
gained: The tunnel gave western Switzerland a direct rail link to Italy. It was the longest rail tunnel in the world at its opening.
The HLS says the Simplon treaty and the tunnel works started new feeder railways, for example the Lötschberg line.
lost: Travel over the Simplon pass road collapsed. The number of travellers went from 13,258 in 1905 to 845 in 1907.
The HLS says the villages along the pass road were isolated for a time after the tunnel opened.

stops.title: Under the mountain to Italy
text: This map shows the land four years after the opening. The tunnel starts east of Brig and ends at the station of Iselle in Italy.
The old pass road over the Simplon runs further east, over the mountain.

stops.title: Two tubes
text: Today two tubes run side by side. Trains from Bern and Geneva use them on the way to Milan.

title: Albula railway Thusis–St. Moritz
place: Rhaetian Railway from Thusis through the Schin gorge, Filisur, Bergün and the Albula tunnel to St. Moritz
summary: From 1898 to 1904 the Rhaetian Railway built a metre-gauge mountain line over the Albula with spirals and an Albula tunnel, to link the Upper Engadine with Chur.
why: In the late 19th century St. Moritz grew into a resort, with four grand hotels in 1900. Regular transport, also in winter, became necessary for the mountain people and for tourism. A planned eastern Alpine railway was never built.

The Rhaetian Railway, under control of the canton, started the work in 1898. The line opened in stages in 1903 and 1904. It was designed for steam trains with limited slopes, so it needed many structures: 42 tunnels and covered galleries and 144 viaducts and bridges. Between Bergün and Preda it climbs in three single spirals and one triple spiral.
In 2008 UNESCO listed the Albula and Bernina lines as a World Heritage site, for the railway and its landscape.
gained: The line opened the Upper Engadine all year. ICOMOS says it supported a strong growth of tourism and the birth of winter sports.
In Bergün the line helped tourism. A spa hotel was built in 1905, and Preda was inhabited all year from then on.
lost: The opening of the Albula line in 1903 brought traffic over the Julier pass largely to a stop.

stops.title: A railway to the Engadine
text: This map shows the line one year after the opening. It runs from Thusis through the Schin gorge and the Albula valley.
After Preda the Albula tunnel leads under the pass into the Engadine.

stops.title: Spirals above Bergün
text: Between Bergün and Preda the valley rises fast. The line turns in spirals and loops to gain height with a gentle slope.

stops.title: A World Heritage line
text: Today the line is part of the UNESCO World Heritage site Rhaetian Railway in the Albula / Bernina Landscapes.

A search summary of HLS Surmeir says the population fell sharply after 1903; not opened, left out.

title: Lötschberg railway and Lötschberg tunnel
place: Kander valley from Frutigen via Kandersteg, 14.6 km tunnel to Goppenstein, south ramp to Brig
summary: From 1906 to 1913 the BLS company built a mountain railway from Frutigen to Brig with a 14.6 km tunnel, to link Bern directly with the Simplon line.
why: The Simplon treaty of 1895 and the work on the Simplon tunnel started new feeder lines. Bern wanted its own direct link to the Simplon and to Italy. The BLS company (Bern-Lötschberg-Simplon) was founded in 1906 to build the line from Frutigen to Brig.

The tunnel was built in a hurry, and the geology was not studied enough. In 1908 a mass of gravel broke into the tunnel under the Gastern valley. It buried 25 men and two horses. The tunnel was then finished in 1913 with a curve around the accident area.
The line was electric from the start. Its ramps climb at up to 27 per mille (27 m per km).
gained: The line was the last large piece of the western Alpine railways. It linked the Bernese rail network with the Simplon tunnel from 1913.
In 1994 a third rail axis made a piggyback corridor (lorries on trains) through the Lötschberg tunnel. The double track was mostly finished by 1992.
lost: 25 workers died when gravel broke into the tunnel. The HLS says the accident happened during the hurried building of the tunnel.

stops.title: A new line from Bern to the Valais
text: This map shows the line two years after the opening. It climbs the Kander valley in loops, passes Kandersteg and enters the tunnel.
From Goppenstein it runs high above the Rhone valley down to Brig.

stops.title: The curve around the accident
text: The tunnel does not run straight. Under the Gastern valley it bends to the east.
This curve goes around the place where gravel broke into the tunnel in 1908 and buried 25 workers.

stops.title: The mountain line today
text: Since 2007 fast trains use the base tunnel. The mountain line still carries regional trains, car trains and some freight trains.

title: Bernina railway St. Moritz–Tirano
place: From St. Moritz via Pontresina over the Bernina pass and Alp Grüm, down the Val Poschiavo to Tirano (Italy)
summary: The Bernina railway, opened in 1910, crosses the Bernina pass in the open at 2253 m and links the Upper Engadine with Tirano in Italy.
why: Like the Albula line, the Bernina line was built to open up the Upper Engadine and to serve the growing tourism. A planned eastern Alpine railway was never built.

The private Bernina railway company built the line as an electric railway from the start. It follows an existing mountain road. So it has steep slopes of up to 70 per mille (70 m per km) and very tight curves. It crosses the pass in the open at 2253 m and goes down to Tirano at 429 m.
The line has 13 tunnels and galleries and 52 viaducts and bridges. It joined the Rhaetian Railway in the 1940s. Since 2008 it is part of the UNESCO World Heritage site.
gained: The line gave St. Moritz a rail link to Italy from 1910 and helped tourism and winter sports in the Upper Engadine.
ICOMOS says the line has never stopped running, with goods, local passengers and access to winter sports.
lost: The HLS says the Bernina railway, opened in 1910, caused a massive drop in goods transport over the Maloja pass.

stops.title: Over the pass by train
text: This map shows the line two years after the opening. It runs from St. Moritz over the Bernina pass and down the Val Poschiavo to Tirano.

stops.title: Down from Alp Grüm
text: Below Alp Grüm the line falls steeply in tight loops to Cavaglia.

stops.title: A World Heritage line
text: Today regional trains and the Bernina Express use the line all year.

title: First Swiss motorway, Lucerne–Ennethorw
place: South of Lucerne, from Kriens past Horw to Ennethorw
summary: In 1955 the canton of Lucerne opened a 3 km road without crossings around Horw, today seen as the first motorway in Switzerland.
why: After the Second World War the number of cars grew fast. In 1950 Switzerland had only 147,000 cars; ten years later there were three and a half times as many. Lucerne wanted a faster link to the tourist places of Central Switzerland and of the canton of Bern.
The canton of Lucerne paid for the road itself. On 11 June 1955 it opened a four-lane bypass of Horw, about 3 km long, between Kriens and Ennethorw. Today it is part of the A2.

The road was simple: there were almost no markings, hard shoulders or crash barriers, and the entries were very short. From 2004 to 2013 the motorway between Lucerne and Hergiswil was rebuilt, partly in tunnels.
gained: Lucerne got a fast road without crossings to the south.
The road was the start of motorway building in Switzerland, before the national road law of 1960.
lost: The motorway was built across the open fields of the Nidfeld between Kriens and Horw (swisstopo maps of 1950 and 1965).
In the first years horse carts and farm vehicles also used the road, and safety equipment was missing.
The rebuilding between Lucerne and Hergiswil (2004–2013) cost about 630 million francs.

title: Great St Bernard road tunnel
place: Under the Great St Bernard Pass, from Bourg-Saint-Bernard (Valais) to the Aosta valley (Italy)
summary: The first road tunnel through the Alps gave the Valais and the Aosta valley a link that stays open in winter.
why: The road over the Great St Bernard Pass cannot be used in winter. A first attempt to dig a road tunnel started in 1850. It stopped after about 100 m on the Swiss side and 70 m on the Italian side.

In 1946 a committee in Martigny began to push for a tunnel. It took twelve years to overcome great financial and political problems. Work started in spring 1958 on the Italian side and soon after on the Swiss side. A Swiss and an Italian company built and still run the tunnel.
The tunnel opened on 19 March 1964. It is 5.798 km long and has one tube. At its opening it was called the first road tunnel through the Alps.
gained: The tunnel gave a winter-safe link between the Valais and the Aosta valley.
In the first year 300,000 motor vehicles used the tunnel. In 1999, when the Mont Blanc tunnel was closed after a fire, 800,000 vehicles used it.
The Aosta valley overcame its winter isolation. In 2022, 849,570 vehicles used the tunnel.
lost: In 2017 a 300 kg beam fell inside the tunnel. The tunnel was closed for three months. The renovation was estimated at 52 million euros.
The future is uncertain: the operating concession ends in 2034, and the two states disagree about the financing.

stops.title: Only a summer road
text: In 1960 the only road went over the pass at 2469 m. Snow closed it every winter.
The blue line shows where the tunnel was being dug from 1958.

stops.title: A road under the pass
text: Since 1964 the tunnel is open all year. The pass road above is still closed in winter.
Today nearly 850,000 vehicles per year use the tunnel.

The northern part of the tunnel lies close to the old pass road on the map; the trace follows the dashed tunnel line, not the road. Traced length about 5.9 km against 5.798 km in the source. Checked on the maps of 1960 (no tunnel yet), 1970 and today. The covered approach road on the Swiss side was not drawn. title: A1 Geneva–Lausanne and the national road network
place: Along Lake Geneva from Geneva past Nyon, Rolle and Morges to Lausanne
summary: One of the first sections of the national motorway network, opened for the Expo 64 exhibition, crossed the vineyards and fields of the La Côte region.
why: In the 1940s planners wanted a road cross for through traffic, from Lake Constance to Geneva and from Basel to Chiasso. A federal commission prepared the laws and the money in 1954–1958. The money was to come mainly from the federal tax on motor fuel.

The national road law came into force in 1960. Parliament approved a network of 1811 km, 800 km of it as motorways. The first sections were the A2 near Hergiswil (1962) and the A1 Geneva–Lausanne, opened in 1963 for the national exhibition Expo 64.
The building took longer and cost more than planned. Most motorways were built between 1965 and 1975. From the early 1970s people opposed parts of the plan; some sections were blocked or removed.
gained: Fast through roads without crossings. By 1980 more than 80% of the network was planned as four-lane motorways.
In 2010, 1790 km of the national road network were in use, 94.6% of the planned length.
lost: The motorway was built across vineyards and fields between Nyon, Rolle and Morges (swisstopo maps of 1960 and 1966).
The cost estimate of 1960 was 3.8 billion francs. By about 2010 the federal state had spent about 61 billion francs on building national roads.
Car numbers grew faster than planned: the number forecast for 1980 was already passed in 1965.
From the early 1970s critics said the planning was undemocratic and did not care enough about people and the environment.

stops.title: Before the motorway
text: In 1960 traffic between Geneva and Lausanne used the old main road along the lake. The blue line shows where the motorway was built, mostly a little above the lake through vineyards and fields.

stops.title: Ready for Expo 64
text: By 1966 the motorway is on the map. It was opened for the national exhibition Expo 64 in Lausanne.
It was one of the first sections of the national road network.

stops.title: Part of a national network
text: Today the A1 is part of a national road network that was about 1790 km long in 2010.

title: San Bernardino road tunnel (A13)
place: Under the San Bernardino Pass, between Hinterrhein and the village of San Bernardino
summary: A 6.6 km tunnel of the A13 linked the Misox (Mesolcina) all year with the rest of Graubünden.
why: Since the Second World War the San Bernardino pass road has been closed in winter. Then the Misox, the Italian-speaking valley south of the pass, had no road link with the rest of the canton.

The tunnel was built as part of the national road N13 (today A13). Drilling began in 1962; in October 1962 about 500 miners worked day and night. The tunnel was broken through on 10 April 1965 and opened on 1 December 1967. It was the first Alpine road tunnel entirely in Switzerland.
The tunnel brought a new rise in traffic over the San Bernardino. After the Gotthard road tunnel opened in 1980, the share of international transit fell again.
gained: Since 1967 the Misox is linked with the rest of the canton all year.
Ticino and Graubünden got a road link that is open all year.
The tunnel brought a new rise in transit traffic to the valleys on the route.
lost: The new rise in traffic was not undisputed, says the federal inventory of historic routes.

title: Gotthard road tunnel (A2)
place: Under the Gotthard massif from Göschenen (Uri) to Airolo (Ticino)
summary: A 16.9 km motorway tunnel gave Ticino a road link that is open all year and made the Gotthard the main road route through the Alps.
why: Snow often cut Ticino off when the Gotthard pass was closed in winter. In 1960 parliament asked for a winter-safe road link to Ticino.

Parliament decided to build the tunnel in 1965. In 1964 it had been added to the national road network. The tunnel has one tube for both directions and four ventilation shafts. The main tunnel was broken through on 3 December 1976.
The tunnel opened on 5 September 1980. It cost 686 million francs. Since then car traffic has left the old pass road, and lorry traffic through the tunnel grew fast.
gained: Ticino got a road link to the north that stays open in winter.
Since 1980 most car traffic uses the tunnel and no longer the pass road.
The tunnel became a main route for passengers and freight between northern and southern Europe.
lost: Lorry traffic grew from 171,000 lorries in 1981 to more than 1.1 million in 1999. The transit traffic became a dispute between Switzerland and the European Union.
In 2001 a serious accident in the tunnel raised concern about the safety of Alpine road tunnels.
At busy times long queues form. On the Palm Sunday weekend of 2000 vehicles queued for more than 32 hours.

Second tube: HLS (law revised 2014, vote 28 February 2016, one direction per tube). Several web pages say 19 workers died while building the tunnel; no primary source was found, so it is not used.

title: Furka base tunnel
place: Metre-gauge rail tunnel from Oberwald (Goms, VS) to Realp (Urseren, UR)
summary: The 15.4 km Furka base tunnel, opened in 1982, lets the trains between the Valais and Uri run all year, with car loading.
why: The Furka-Oberalp railway reached Disentis in 1926. Its line over the Furka ran through a short summit tunnel. The trains could not run there in winter.
From 1973 to 1982 the 15.4 km Furka base tunnel was built, with a side tunnel to the south into the Bedretto valley. It cost 311 million francs. The tunnel opened in June 1982.
gained: The tunnel allowed the railway to run all year, with car loading.
lost: The old mountain line over the Furka was closed. In 1987 the Dampfbahn Furka-Bergstrecke (a volunteer steam railway) took it over and reopened it step by step as a tourist railway.

stops.title: Over the pass in summer only
text: In 1981 the trains still went from Oberwald via Gletsch and a summit tunnel to Realp. In winter this line was closed.
The blue line shows the base tunnel, which opened one year later.

stops.title: All year through the mountain
text: Today trains and car trains run all year through the base tunnel. In summer steam trains run again on the old line over the pass.

title: Vereina tunnel
place: Rhaetian Railway tunnel from Klosters (Selfranga, Prättigau) to Sagliains near Lavin (Lower Engadine)
summary: The Vereina tunnel of the Rhaetian Railway, opened in 1999, gives the Lower Engadine a rail and car-train link that stays open in winter.
why: From the north, the Lower Engadine was reached by road over the Flüela pass. The tunnel was planned as a link that is safe in winter, instead of the Flüela pass road.

The work started in 1991. The tunnel opened on 19 November 1999. With a little more than 19 km it is the longest metre-gauge rail tunnel in the world. It was the first extension of the Rhaetian Railway network since its founding period.
In 1985 the cost was estimated at 538 million francs. In the end it cost about 800 million francs.
gained: The Lower Engadine came much closer to the Swiss Plateau. The travel time from Zurich to Scuol was halved.
The car trains (the 'rolling road') give the region a road link that is safe in winter. In 2019 more than half a million drivers used the car trains for the first time.
lost: In the Prättigau people feared a flood of cars ('Blechlawine'). Environmental groups objected to the car trains.
The tunnel cost about 800 million francs instead of the 538 million estimated in 1985.

stops.title: Over the Flüela pass
text: In 1990 the road over the Flüela pass was the direct way from the north into the Lower Engadine.
The blue line shows where the Vereina tunnel would run.

stops.title: Through the mountain all year
text: Today trains and car trains run through the tunnel all year. The Flüela pass road is still used in summer.

title: Gotthard and Ceneri base tunnels (NEAT)
place: Gotthard base tunnel from Erstfeld (UR) to Bodio (TI); Ceneri base tunnel from Camorino to Vezia near Lugano
summary: Two long flat tunnels deep under the mountains let trains cross the Alps without steep ramps: the 57 km Gotthard base tunnel (2016) and the 15.4 km Ceneri base tunnel (2020).
why: Switzerland lies on one of the main freight routes of Europe. About 26 million tonnes of goods cross the Swiss Alps by rail each year, 80% of it transit. In several votes the people decided to move freight across the Alps from the road to the rail. In 1992 the voters accepted the NEAT project (new rail links through the Alps).

The main digging of the Gotthard base tunnel started in 1999. About 2400 people worked on the sites at peak times, in three shifts. Tunnel boring machines dug 80% of the main tubes, blasting the rest. The rock had up to 50 °C. The tunnel opened for regular trains on 11 December 2016. Its highest point is only 550 m above sea level.
The Ceneri base tunnel south of Bellinzona completed the flat line. It opened on 4 September 2020 and cost about 3.6 billion francs. South of Lugano, trains still use a line from 1874.
gained: The flat line allows longer and heavier freight trains with fewer locomotives. Up to 260 freight trains a day can use the Gotthard base tunnel; the old mountain line allowed a maximum of 180.
The tunnel shortens the line from Altdorf to Bellinzona by 30 km. After the whole axis was finished, travellers from Zurich to Lugano save about 45 minutes.
With the Ceneri base tunnel, the trip from Bellinzona to Lugano went from 27 to 19 minutes, and from Lugano to Locarno from 50 to 29 minutes.
lost: Nine tunnel workers died during the building of the Gotthard base tunnel. All came from abroad.
The digging brought 28.2 million tonnes of rock out of the Gotthard base tunnel. This spoil (dug-out rock) had to be stored or used elsewhere.
The Gotthard base tunnel cost about 12.2 billion francs in total; the whole NEAT cost a little more than 23 billion francs.

stops.title: The old way over the mountain
text: In 1885 trains climbed up the valleys to the Gotthard tunnel at about 1150 m. The red line shows the tunnel of 1882.
The blue lines show where the base tunnels run today, deep under the mountains.

stops.title: A flat line through the Alps
text: The Gotthard base tunnel runs 57 km from Erstfeld to Bodio. With up to 2300 m of rock above it, it is the deepest rail tunnel in the world.
Further south, the Ceneri base tunnel runs 15.4 km from Camorino to Vezia near Lugano.

title: Lötschberg base tunnel (NEAT)
place: Base tunnel from Frutigen (BE) to Raron (VS)
summary: The Lötschberg base tunnel, opened in 2007, runs about 35 km from Frutigen to Raron, deep under the old Lötschberg line.
why: In 1992 the voters accepted the NEAT project with base tunnels through the Lötschberg and the Gotthard. The aim was a faster rail link through the Alps and more freight on rail instead of on the road.
Base tunnels have been built on the transit axes since 1999. The BLS put the Lötschberg base tunnel into service on 15 June 2007. It was the first NEAT base tunnel to open.
Only part of the tunnel was equipped with two tracks. On 21 of its almost 35 km the trains can use only one track.
gained: The Valais and northern Italy came more than one hour closer to the Swiss Plateau. Daily crossings rose from about 7600 to more than 13,000 people.
In 2016 a new record of more than 33 million gross tonnes went through the tunnel.
lost: Because 21 km are single-track, the tunnel reached its capacity limit only ten years after the opening (BLS, 2017).

stops.title: The old line over the top
text: In 1915 the trains climbed to the tunnel of 1913 at Kandersteg (red line).
The blue line shows the base tunnel of 2007. It runs further west and much lower, from Frutigen straight to the Rhone valley.

stops.title: Under the mountains
text: Today fast trains from Bern reach Visp in the Valais through the base tunnel. The old line stays in use for regional trains and car trains.
